name: Harun al-Rashid
info: Harun al-Rashid was the fifth Abbasid caliph, who reigned from 786 to 809; his reign is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the Islamic Golden Age and is remembered through the One Thousand and One Nights.

facts.born: Between 763 and 766 (17 March 763 and February 766 are the most probable dates), at Rey in Jibal, in present-day Iran; son of the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi and al-Khayzuran
facts.died: 24 March 809, of an illness, at Sanabad village in Tus, Khorasan, while marching against the rebel Rafi ibn al-Layth; buried there in the Dar al-Imarah
facts.role: Nominal leader of campaigns against the Byzantines, 780 and 782; crown prince and governor of the empire's western territories, from Syria to Azerbaijan; fifth Abbasid caliph, September 786 – March 809
facts.known: A reign traditionally seen as the start of the Islamic Golden Age; the Bayt al-Hikma ("House of Wisdom") in Baghdad; campaigns against Byzantium; the exchange of embassies and gifts with Charlemagne; the fall of the Barmakids; his place in the One Thousand and One Nights

t: Harun al-Rashid became caliph in 786, in his early twenties, with the help of his mother al-Khayzuran and of Yahya ibn Khalid the Barmakid, whose family then ran the administration for seventeen years.
Under him the Abbasid empire reached its peak and Baghdad flourished, while he fought Byzantium, exchanged embassies with Charlemagne and put down Kharijite and Alid revolts.
He destroyed the Barmakids, imprisoned Alid leaders, and divided the succession between his sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun, who went to war after his death.
dyk: In 802 Harun sent Charlemagne an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock that marked the hours by dropping bronze balls into a bowl while mechanical knights, one for each hour, came out of little doors. Charlemagne and his retinue took the clock for a conjuration.
ev: Harun nominally leads an expedition against the Byzantines that reaches the Asian suburbs of Constantinople, and is given the name al-Rashid
On the death of his brother al-Hadi he becomes the fifth Abbasid caliph, with Yahya ibn Khalid the Barmakid as vizier
The Alid Yahya ibn Abdallah proclaims a revolt in Daylam, and Harun has his son Muhammad sworn in as heir with the name al-Amin
He moves the court and government from Baghdad to Raqqa on the middle Euphrates
He recognises Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab as semi-autonomous emir of Ifriqiya in exchange for an annual payment
He sends Charlemagne an elephant and a water clock, and the new Byzantine emperor Nikephoros I refuses him tribute
By al-Tabari's dating, he has Ja'far the Barmakid executed and the rest of the family imprisoned
He dies at Tus in Khorasan while marching against the rebel Rafi ibn al-Layth, and al-Amin succeeds him

sections.early:
Abū Jaʿfar Hārūn ibn Muḥammad was born at Rey, then part of Jibal in the Abbasid Caliphate, in present-day Iran. The date is debated: sources give years from 763 to 766, with 17 March 763 and February 766 the most probable. His father was al-Mahdi, the third Abbasid caliph, who reigned from 775 to 785; his mother, al-Khayzuran, was a woman of strong and independent personality who greatly influenced affairs of state in the reigns of her husband and her sons.

Growing up, Harun studied history, geography, rhetoric, music, poetry and economics, but most of his time went to mastering hadith and the Quran. He was also trained in swordplay, archery and the art of war. The court he was raised in defined orthodoxy by force: al-Mahdi held that the caliph had the responsibility to define the orthodox theology of Muslims, ordered polemical works against freethinkers and heretics, and for years had those suspected of being zindiqs, or dualists, hunted down and put to death in large numbers.

In 780 and again in 782, before he was caliph, Harun nominally led campaigns against the caliphate's traditional enemy, the Eastern Roman Empire, then ruled by the empress Irene. The second expedition was a huge undertaking that reached the Asian suburbs of Constantinople. According to the Muslim chronicler al-Tabari, the Byzantines lost tens of thousands of soldiers and Harun used 20,000 mules to carry the riches back. In 781–82 he married Zubaidah, the daughter of his paternal uncle Ja'far and a granddaughter of al-Mansur, the founder of Baghdad.
sections.rise:
The raids raised Harun's political standing. On his return he was given the laqab al-Rashid, "the Rightly-Guided One", was promoted to crown prince, and was made governor of the empire's western territories, from Syria to Azerbaijan. When al-Mahdi died in 785, Harun's brother al-Hadi became caliph. Al-Hadi reigned for a year and two months. He clashed with their mother over her influence at court, where commanders and petitioners lined up at her door, and threatened to behead any of his men found there; al-Khayzuran swore never to speak to him again and left the palace. He also tried to depose Harun as crown prince in favour of his own son Ja'far, while their mother favoured Harun.

Al-Tabari notes varying accounts of al-Hadi's death in 786, among them an abdominal ulcer and an assassination prompted by his mother. That night al-Khayzuran released Yahya ibn Khalid from prison and ordered him to pay the army's wages, send letters to the governors and prepare Harun as caliph. The commander Khuzayma ibn Khazim reportedly armed 5,000 of his followers, dragged Ja'far ibn al-Hadi from his bed and forced him to renounce his claim publicly.

Harun became caliph in his early twenties. He named Yahya, his mentor and of the Barmakid family, vizier with full executive powers; Yahya and his sons served him for seventeen years. Until her death in 789 al-Khayzuran acted as an overseer of affairs, and Yahya deferred to her advice. Harun released many of the Umayyads and Alids his brother had imprisoned and declared an amnesty for all political groups of the Quraysh.
sections.deeds:
Under Harun the Abbasid empire reached its peak. Baghdad flourished as a centre of knowledge, culture and trade, and tribute paid by many rulers funded architecture, the arts and court luxuries; he is credited with establishing the library Bayt al-Hikma, the "House of Wisdom". In 796 he moved the court to Raqqa on the middle Euphrates, close to the Byzantine border and well connected to Baghdad and Damascus, and spent twelve years there. He gave the jurist Abu Yusuf the title of Grand Qadi, the first time it was conferred, with the power to appoint other judges. He made the pilgrimage to Mecca several times, the last in 803.

Large-scale hostilities broke out with Byzantium. When Nikephoros I became emperor in 802 and refused to pay tribute, Harun wrote his answer on the back of the emperor's letter, addressing him as "dog of the Romans"; after campaigns in Asia Minor Nikephoros was forced to accept a treaty on humiliating terms. A Frankish mission came to offer friendship in 799, and Einhard and Notker the Stammerer describe envoys travelling between Harun and Charlemagne to discuss Christian access to holy sites. In 802 Harun sent silks, ivory chessmen, an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock. He also sent embassies to Tang China, with which an alliance against the Tibetans was established.

In 800 he recognised Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab as emir of Ifriqiya, semi-autonomous in exchange for 40,000 gold dinars a year. Al-Tabari reports the saying that at Harun's death the state treasury held more than nine hundred million dirhams.
sections.opponents:
The reign saw repeated revolts. In 794 the Kharijite al-Walid ibn Tarif overran much of the Jazira and defeated two armies sent against him, until Yazid ibn Mazyad al-Shaybani killed him in single combat in late 795. The Alid Yahya ibn Abdallah proclaimed a revolt in Daylam in 792. Harun sent the Barmakid al-Fadl ibn Yahya with 50,000 men, and Yahya surrendered in return for a letter of pardon written in the caliph's own hand. Harun remained suspicious. He later had Yahya brought back to Baghdad and held in prison or under house arrest, and convened jurists to reassess the pardon; when Muhammad al-Shaybani declared it inviolable, the caliph threw his inkstand at him, and another judge declared it invalid and cut it with a knife. According to Shia belief, Harun also imprisoned and poisoned Musa ibn Ja'far, the seventh Imam, who died in a Baghdad prison in 799.

The fall of the Barmakids is the most debated act of his reign. The family was imprisoned and its lands confiscated in 798, or by al-Tabari's dating in 803, and Ja'far ibn Yahya was executed; one account links the brutal manner of his death to his having let Yahya ibn Abdallah escape. The true causes are not known with certainty; it may be that Harun wanted to rid himself of a group that could limit his own power.

In Khurasan the governor Ali ibn Isa oppressed the province through heavy taxation and amassed a vast fortune. When Harun went to Rayy in April 805 to investigate the complaints, Ali brought an enormous treasure, and the caliph kept him in place.
sections.last:
Ali ibn Isa's misconduct in Khurasan ended in a major rebellion under Rafi ibn al-Layth, which began in Samarqand. Harun dismissed and arrested Ali and replaced him with Harthama ibn A'yan, but the revolt continued unchecked, and in 808 the caliph marched east himself. He fell ill and died soon after reaching the village of Sanabad in Tus, on 24 March 809. He was buried in the Dar al-Imarah, the summer palace of Humayd ibn Qahtaba, the Abbasid governor of Khorasan. Shortly before his death he is said to have been reading lines by the poet Abu al-Atahiya on the transitory nature of the power and pleasures of this world, an anecdote also told of other caliphs. Inan, a singer and poet among his concubines, accompanied him to Khurasan and died there soon after him.

The succession had been arranged long before. His son Abdallah, the future al-Ma'mun, was born in September 786, on the night of his accession, to Marajil, a Persian concubine who died in the birth; Muhammad, born about six months later to his wife Zubaidah, took precedence because both his parents were Abbasids. In 792 Harun had Muhammad receive the oath of allegiance under the name al-Amin, "the Trustworthy". Abdallah was named second heir, as al-Ma'mun, "the Trusted One", only in 799, and a third son, al-Qasim, was nominated third heir. Both elder heirs grew up at Raqqa.

Al-Amin succeeded his father in 809 and ruled until 813. When he tried to remove al-Ma'mun, then governor of Khorasan, as his heir, civil war broke out between the brothers. Al-Ma'mun became caliph in 813 and ruled until 833.
sections.legacy:
Harun's reign is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the Islamic Golden Age. All the Abbasid caliphs after him were his descendants: al-Amin and al-Ma'mun were followed by another of his sons, Abu Ishaq Muhammad, better known as al-Mu'tasim, whose mother was the concubine Marida. Harun is sometimes accused of weakening the Abbasid legacy by dividing the central powers of the realm between two sons, which created the tension that led to war between them. The place where he was buried later became known as Mashhad, "the Place of Martyrdom", after the martyrdom there of Imam al-Ridha in 818.

The historian al-Masudi wrote that the splendour, riches and prosperity of the reign were such that the period was called "the Honeymoon", and the poet and musician al-Mawsili likened his accession to the sun coming out of hiding. Many anecdotes attached themselves to Harun in the centuries after his rule: al-Masudi relates a number in The Meadows of Gold, and Saadi of Shiraz put others into his Gulistan.

Portions of the One Thousand and One Nights are set at his court, some of its stories involve Harun himself, and the character of King Shahryar may have been based on him. Because of these tales he became a legendary figure, which has obscured his historical personality. He appears in poems by Alfred Tennyson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and W. B. Yeats, in James Joyce's Ulysses, and in the names of the two protagonists of Salman Rushdie's Haroun and the Sea of Stories. He has been described as one of the most famous Arabs in history.

summary: Harun al-Rashid ruled the Abbasid Caliphate from 786 to 809, when the empire reached its peak and Baghdad flourished. He fought Byzantium, exchanged gifts with Charlemagne, destroyed the Barmakid family that had governed for him, and left a divided succession. The One Thousand and One Nights made him a figure of legend.
references: André Clot, Harun Al-Rashid and the Age of a Thousand and One Nights (New Amsterdam Books, 1990)
Benson Bobrick, The Caliph's Splendor: Islam and the West in the Golden Age of Baghdad (Simon & Schuster, 2012)
Nabia Abbott, Two Queens of Baghdad: Mother and Wife of Hārūn Al Rashīd (University of Chicago Press, 1946)
Masudi, The Meadows of Gold: The Abbasids (Routledge, 2013)
notes: Birth year: the lead gives 'c. 763 or 766'; the body 'from 763 to 766'; the timeline 'from 763 to 768', with 17 March 763 and February 766 most probable. start set to 763, circa true.

The article's 'Timeline of important events' is unreliable and I did not use its entries for 802 ('two albino elephants'), 805 (Battle of Krasos), 807 (Cyprus) or 809 ('Abdurrahman Ad-Dakhil in Cyprus ... died on 30 November', which contradicts 24 March 809 and looks like vandalism). I did take from it the two most probable birth dates and Musa al-Kazim's death in a Baghdad prison in 799; the date 14 September 786 for al-Hadi's death is there too but I gave only the year.

Fall of the Barmakids: the article says 'until 798, when the caliph threw them in prison', then 'Al-Tabari dates this event to 803', and elsewhere places it after the Hajj of 802. Both dates are given; the event list uses al-Tabari's 803.

Internal inconsistencies left out: Abdallah ibn Mus'ab 'died on the same day (29 March 809)' in an episode dated 800; 'Many Alids managed to escape the battle' (the battle is never named; it is Fakhkh); Idris founding his dynasty in 789 while the narrative has the brothers separating later.
Bayt al-Hikma: the lead says Harun 'established the legendary library'; I wrote 'he is credited with establishing'.

Raqqa: 'where he spent 12 years, most of his reign' and 'visited Baghdad only once' sit beside pilgrimages 'from Baghdad'; I gave the twelve years only. The later move of the court to al-Rayy (c. 804-805) is mentioned only through the April 805 visit.

Zubaidah: called daughter of his paternal uncle Ja'far in Family and 'a granddaughter of al-Mansur' in Caliphate; both used. The article says al-Ma'mun was 'six months older' than al-Amin; I wrote 'about six months later'.
Charlemagne: the lead says the Frankish mission came in 799; the Diplomacy section dates the gifts to 802. The chessmen, elephant and clock are from the 802 list.
Death: the article gives no illness by name. '24 March 809' is from the lead; the body says 'March 809'.

Religious policy sentence in the article is garbled ('continued the pogroms, although with diminished intensity ... and was later abolished by him, Harun kept the ban on heretics but stopped the execution of every heretic'); I described only al-Mahdi's policy, in 'early', and left Harun's own policy out as unclear.

Wanted but not in the article: the year he was made crown prince; details and years of his own Byzantine campaigns as caliph (e.g. 806 Heraclea is mentioned only in passing under Family); the Mecca succession arrangement; the cause of death; the founding date of the Bayt al-Hikma.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
